where $\mathbf{v}_{n,c}$ is the bulk velocity of the cold neutral population, $\hat{\ell}$ is the selected line-of-sight unit vector, and $v_{n,c,\ell}$ is the signed projected velocity. The projection is the velocity represented by the Doppler centroid of the corresponding cold-neutral emission component.

This quantity is distinct from [hot neutral velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity), which describes the energetic neutral population, and from [neutral internal state velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity), which is resolved for a specified internal state. It excludes thermal speed and velocity spread, which are higher moments of the velocity distribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the cold-neutral bulk velocity points along the chosen positive line-of-sight unit vector $\hat{\ell}$.

items.name: radial_neutral_particle_flux
items.description: Radial neutral particle flux is the signed net number flow per unit area and time toward increasing major radius for one neutral atomic or molecular species, summed over its internal states. It is the cylindrical major-radius component, not the flux-surface-normal component.
items.documentation:
Radial neutral particle flux is the signed component of neutral particle-number transport in the direction of increasing major radius. It gives the net number flow per area and time for one neutral atomic or molecular species, with that species’ internal states combined.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, its defining projection and internal-state aggregation are:

$$
\Gamma_{0,R} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}} = \sum_a \Gamma_{0,a,R}
$$

where $\Gamma_{0,R}$ is the radial neutral particle flux, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0$ is the [neutral particle flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) for one species summed over its internal states, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius, $a$ indexes the internal states of that species, and $\Gamma_{0,a,R}$ is its [radial neutral internal-state particle flux](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_particle_flux). Here, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one neutral species, includes all its internal states, and does not sum over distinct neutral species or include charged particles. It is a flux density, not a surface-integrated particle rate. A flux-surface-averaged transport value is the average of this radial component over the surface; the major-radius direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface, so this average is not the flux-surface-normal component.

This is the major-radius projection of [neutral particle flux](name:neutral_particle_flux), and summing the state-resolved radial contributions gives the species-level quantity. [Poloidal neutral particle flux](name:poloidal_neutral_particle_flux) and [parallel neutral particle flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux) are distinct directional projections of neutral particle transport. The flux-surface-averaged form represents radial neutral transport in the neutral particle balance.

Sign convention: Positive when the net neutral particle flux has a component toward increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

items.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential
items.description: Radial component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for a linear MHD mode, retaining its signed projection toward increasing major radius.
items.documentation:
Radial component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction associated with a linear MHD mode.

The radial component is defined by

$$
\delta A_R = \delta\mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $\delta A_R$ is the radial component, $\delta\mathbf{A}$ is the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity represents one signed component of the plasma perturbation about a reference state; it is not the complete vector, a magnitude, a sum, or an average. The complete vector quantity is the [perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential), while the [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential) provides an adjacent directional component. It includes the full radial eigenfunction rather than selecting only its real or imaginary quadrature; the latter is represented by the [radial perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part).

The associated perturbed magnetic field $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is obtained from the curl relation $\delta\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{A}$, where $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic field and $\nabla\times$ is the spatial curl operator. The vector potential is gage-dependent, whereas its curl determines the corresponding magnetic-field perturbation.

Sign convention: Positive when $\delta A_R$ points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

items.name: ion_particle_convection_velocity
items.description: Effective advective ion transport velocity whose product with ion number density gives the convective particle flux, excluding density-gradient-driven diffusion.
items.documentation:
Ion particle convection velocity is the effective vector coefficient of the density-proportional advective ion particle flux. It represents directed particle transport after density-gradient-driven diffusion has been separated.

The convective ion particle flux is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_i\mathbf{v}_i
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective ion particle flux, $n_i$ is the number density of the specified ion population, and $\mathbf{v}_i$ is its particle convection velocity; the subscript $i$ denotes ions.

For a specified ion species, the density is summed over all ionic charge states, excluding neutral particles, and the velocity is the density-weighted mean over all charge states rather than a sum of velocities. The [ion charge-state particle convection velocity](name:ion_charge_state_particle_convection_velocity) instead applies to a specified charge state. This quantity describes particle transport, not heat or momentum transport, and need not equal the ion fluid velocity. It is not restricted to the edge plasma or to a particular transport direction.

The [parallel ion particle convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_particle_convection_velocity) is its magnetic-field-aligned projection. The [radial ion particle convection velocity](name:radial_ion_particle_convection_velocity) is its major-radius projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The [effective ion particle convection velocity](name:effective_ion_particle_convection_velocity) specializes to transport across magnetic flux surfaces; that direction need not coincide with the cylindrical radial direction.

Sign convention: Positive when a projected convection velocity points along its defining positive direction: toward increasing $R$ for the cylindrical radial component, or along the magnetic field for the parallel component.

items.name: co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
items.description: Volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface.
items.documentation:
Co-passing thermal-electron collisional power density is the signed rate of kinetic-energy transfer from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. The orbit restriction applies to the donating fast-particle distribution, not to the receiving thermal electrons.

It is defined by the thermal-electron kinetic-energy moment of the corresponding Coulomb collision operator:

$$
P_{\mathrm{e,co}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left\langle \sum_a \int \frac{1}{2}m_{\mathrm e}|\mathbf v|^2 C_{\mathrm ea}[f_{\mathrm e}^{\mathrm{th}},f_a^{\mathrm{co}}] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{e,co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this collisional power density, $m_{\mathrm e}$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf v$ is electron velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The index $a$ runs over the fast species represented by the donating distribution; $f_{\mathrm e}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the bulk thermal-electron velocity distribution, and $f_a^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the fast-species distribution restricted to co-passing guiding-center orbits. The operator $C_{\mathrm ea}$ gives the collisional rate of change of the thermal-electron distribution caused by that fast-species contribution. Angle brackets denote the volume-shell-weighted flux-surface average, and $\psi$ labels the averaging surface.

This quantity is an energy source or sink, not stored thermal-electron energy. It excludes energy transferred to ions or suprathermal electrons and excludes the counter-passing and trapped parts of the donating distribution.

With the same flux-surface averaging applied to every term, this contribution, the [counter-passing contribution](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), and the [trapped contribution](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) sum to the orbit-unrestricted [thermal-electron collisional power density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net kinetic energy from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal electrons.

items.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
items.description: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its inner conducting boundary. It is nonnegative.
items.documentation:
Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,phi,Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to its inner conducting boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The inner boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected inner-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R_i - R_c)^2 + (Z_i - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annular cross-section center and $(R_i,Z_i)$ is the inner-boundary position in the same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This quantity specializes [radius_of_passive_loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) to the inner conducting boundary and complements [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). For a circular annulus, the conductor thickness is the outer radius minus this inner radius, and [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is determined by the difference of the squared outer and inner radii. It is a cross-sectional size, not the loop center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

items.name: radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position
items.description: Major-radius coordinate of a measurement position, equal to its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
items.documentation:
Major-radius coordinate of measurement position

The coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates of the same position in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, whose origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis and whose vertical coordinate $z$ is aligned with $Z$.

This quantity evaluates the parent coordinate at the specified measurement position; no summation, averaging, or weighting is implied. It is nonnegative and vanishes on the toroidal symmetry axis. It is distinct from a minor-radius distance measured from the magnetic axis and from a magnetic flux label.

The [radial coordinate of a line of sight](name:radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight) specifically locates that line's second reference point; this quantity does not impose that reference-point convention.

items.name: inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
items.description: Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the bore-side radius of an annular conductor or winding-pack cross-section, measured from the geometric center of that cross-section to its inner boundary.
items.documentation:
Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the non-negative radial distance in the local cross-sectional plane normal to the local conductor or winding-pack centerline, from the geometric center of an annular toroidal-field-coil cross-section to its bore-side inner boundary. It defines the bore size of the annular cross-section, not the spatial location of the coil.

For an annular cross-section with circular inner and outer boundaries, the conducting or winding-pack cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the annular cross-sectional area in square meters, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is this inner radius in meters, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the corresponding outer radius in meters.

The quantity is defined for hollow annular conductor or winding-pack cross-sections and obeys $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$; the limiting value $r_\mathrm{inner}=0$ represents a solid circular cross-section treated as an annulus with no bore. It is the inner-boundary member of the toroidal-field-coil cross-section radius family: outer_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil gives the outer boundary, while radius_of_toroidal_field_coil denotes a generic non-negative cross-section radius not tied specifically to the bore-side boundary.

items.name: deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
items.description: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of D-D neutron emission per unit volume at each point in the plasma.
items.documentation:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-D fusion reactions. Only the neutron-emitting D-D branch contributes, so this quantity is the local source of prompt fusion neutrons from deuterium-deuterium reactions that produce a neutron.

For identical deuterium reactants, the branch emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DD} = \frac{1}{2} n_D^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}
$$

where $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity, $n_D$ is the local deuterium reactant number density, $\sigma$ is the fusion cross-section for the neutron-emitting D-D branch, $v$ is the relative speed of the deuterium reactants, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the velocity average of $\sigma v$ over the local reactant distributions. The factor $1/2$ avoids double-counting unordered pairs of identical deuterium reactants.

The scope is the D-D reaction channel at a plasma location, aggregated over all deuterium reactant charge states and kinetic populations that contribute to the local neutron-emitting D-D branch unless a component-resolved quantity is specified. It excludes the proton-emitting D-D branch, subsequent D-T neutron production involving tritium born from D-D reactions, and the [deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion). The reaction-pair label deuterium_deuterium denotes two deuterium reactants; it is not a charge-state-resolved fuel-state quantity.

Integrating $\varepsilon_{DD}$ over a plasma volume gives the D-D contribution to the global neutron flux for the same reactant population, and weighting that contribution by the branch neutron energy gives its contribution to total neutron power. When reactant populations are resolved, the corresponding global neutron production can be decomposed into [thermal neutron flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), beam-thermal neutron flux, and beam-beam neutron flux contributions; those are population decompositions of the volume-integrated source, not separate definitions of the local D-D emissivity. Together with [deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity due to fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), this quantity is a reaction-channel-specific member of [neutron emissivity due to fusion](name:neutron_emissivity_due_to_fusion).

items.name: radial_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser
items.description: Major-radius location of the Thomson-scattering laser endpoint, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
items.documentation:
The radial coordinate of a Thomson-scattering laser is the major-radius position of its laser-beam endpoint, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
R_{\mathrm{end}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{end}}^2+y_{\mathrm{end}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the endpoint major-radius coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{end}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the endpoint coordinates along the two horizontal axes of the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one laser endpoint and is a geometric point coordinate, not a path average, scattering-volume coordinate, beam attribute, or plasma-population quantity. It is neither summed nor averaged over lasers, endpoints, or plasma regions.

It is the Thomson-scattering-laser-specific realization of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), providing the $R$ coordinate of the endpoint. It is distinct from the [toroidal coordinate of the Thomson-scattering laser](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser), which specifies the endpoint's toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: energy_diffusion_coefficient
items.description: Fick's-law coefficient relating the diffusive thermal energy flux of a plasma constituent to its local temperature gradient, serving as the species-agnostic parent abstraction over electron, ion, and neutral population specializations.
items.documentation:
The energy diffusion coefficient characterizes gradient-driven thermal energy transport for any plasma constituent — electrons, ions, or neutrals — by specifying the proportionality between the diffusive heat flux and the local temperature gradient in the Fick's-law sense. It is the thermal-energy channel of the general diffusion_coefficient, which governs particle, momentum, and energy transport alike, and it is distinct from convective or $E \times B$ contributions to the total heat flux.

The defining relation for the diffusive energy flux $\mathbf{Q}_\mathrm{diff}$ of a given constituent is:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_\mathrm{diff} = -D_E \, \nabla T
$$

where $D_E$ is the energy diffusion coefficient and $\nabla T$ is the temperature gradient of that constituent. In a magnetized plasma $D_E$ is strongly anisotropic; radial cross-field values govern energy confinement while values along field lines are orders of magnitude larger.

Species-resolved children include [electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for the electron population and [ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for the total ion population aggregated over all charge states; neutral-particle transport is handled by analogous neutral specializations. The effective diffusivity that combines diffusive and convective contributions is tracked separately by energy_effective_diffusivity.

items.name: poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
items.description: Signed poloidal tilt angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from +R.
items.documentation:
The quantity is the signed orientation angle of the normal defining a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive axis. It specifies the probe’s tilt in the poloidal cross-section, rather than the spatial angle of the probe center.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $n_R$ and $n_Z$ denote the components of the probe’s oriented sensitive-axis normal along the increasing-$R$ and increasing-$Z$ directions. The poloidal angle $\theta_{\rm pol}$ is defined by:

$$
\theta_{\rm pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-n_Z,n_R)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument arctangent that preserves the quadrant of the projected normal.

The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe and its oriented sensitive-axis normal. This is a geometric sensor-orientation quantity, not the poloidal coordinate of the probe center, the direction of the measured magnetic field, or a plasma flux-surface coordinate; it has no plasma-population or region aggregation and is not summed over probes or coil windings.

It is a probe-specific application of the parent [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface): the parent defines the geometric angular measure, while this quantity applies it to the probe’s oriented normal. The complementary [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) describes the toroidal orientation of the same probe normal, whereas [poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position) describes the angular location of a measurement point.

Sign convention: Positive when the sensitive-axis normal points from the outward radial direction toward decreasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, following the clockwise direction in the poloidal plane.

items.name: surface_emissivity
items.description: Dimensionless ratio of thermal radiation emitted by a surface to blackbody radiation at the same surface temperature, with the stated spectral and angular averaging.
items.documentation:
Surface emissivity is the effectiveness of a material surface in emitting thermal electromagnetic radiation relative to an ideal blackbody at the same temperature. It is a material property of the emitting surface and is distinct from the emitted energy flux described by [energy flux due to surface emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

The effective emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{M_{\mathrm{emit}}(T_s)}{M_{\mathrm{bb}}(T_s)}
$$

where $M_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the surface thermal radiative exitance, $M_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the blackbody exitance, and $T_s$ is the surface temperature. The ratio applies to the specified spectral band and angular averaging; it is not a wavelength- and direction-resolved emissivity. Incident radiation and geometric surface area, such as optical-element area, are excluded.

items.name: neutral_velocity
items.description: Mean translational velocity of a neutral-particle population, resolved or averaged over internal states and energy ranges, with component projections representing the same bulk flow.
items.documentation:
The neutral velocity is the mean translational flow of a selected neutral-particle population, whether resolved by internal state or energy range or aggregated over several such populations.

At position $\mathbf r$, it is defined by the first velocity moment:

$$
\mathbf{u}_n(\mathbf r)=\frac{\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\int \mathbf v\,f_{n,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}{\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\int f_{n,a}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}
$$

where $\mathbf r$ is position in m, $\mathbf v$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{n,a}$ is phase-space density in m$^{-6}$ s$^3$, $a$ labels included internal-state or energy subpopulations, and $\mathcal A$ is the included set. A resolved form is represented by [neutral internal-state velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity), while aggregation over included states gives a bulk form such as [bulk neutral internal-state velocity](name:bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity). Vertical, poloidal, parallel, cold, and hot variants select projections or population subsets of this same mean flow.

items.name: momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
items.description: Momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed transfer rate of a selected linear-momentum component per surface area, attributed to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport.
items.documentation:
Momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed flux density of a selected component of linear [momentum](name:momentum) attributed to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport. The direction of the transported momentum is distinct from the normal direction of the surface across which it is transferred.

The contribution through an oriented surface is defined by

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf e}_p \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{dia}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is this momentum flux, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the momentum-flux tensor contribution attributed to diamagnetic drift, $\hat{\mathbf e}_p$ is the unit vector selecting the transported momentum component, and $\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the chosen positive unit normal to the transfer surface. The tensor's first index denotes the transported momentum direction and its second index denotes the transport direction.

For the total momentum balance, the contributing population and charge-state fluxes are summed. No particular species, charge state, momentum axis, surface orientation, or plasma region is selected by this general quantity. It is normalized to the actual surface area, not integrated over that area, and excludes contributions from non-diamagnetic transport mechanisms.

The [ion momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [neutral momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:neutral_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) specialize the participating population. Neutral specializations denote momentum transport attributed to this mechanism, not a direct magnetic drift of uncharged particles.

Sign convention: Positive when positive momentum along $\hat{\mathbf e}_p$ is transported through the surface in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf n}$.

items.name: length_variation_of_interferometer_beam
items.description: Signed plasma-induced change in the effective optical path accumulated along an interferometer beam relative to its corresponding no-plasma reference path.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the signed plasma-induced change in effective optical path length accumulated along an electromagnetic propagation path represented by an interferometer beam. It describes an optical delay or advance caused by the plasma, rather than the unperturbed geometric path length.

The variation is defined as

$$
\Delta L = L_{\mathrm{plasma}} - L_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\Delta L$ is the optical path-length variation, $L_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the effective optical path along the beam in the presence of plasma, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding effective path without plasma.

This quantity applies to the net change accumulated along the interferometer beam's complete line of sight. It is a path-integrated optical quantity, not a local path-length density, an unperturbed geometric length, or a separate phase-calibration coefficient. As the variation of [length of an interferometer beam](name:length_of_interferometer_beam), it expresses the plasma-induced departure from the reference path. The associated phase shift provides the optical information used to derive [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density).

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma-affected effective optical path length exceeds the corresponding no-plasma reference path.

items.name: toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
items.description: Toroidal component of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma, resolved for a single toroidal Fourier mode number in linear MHD stability analysis.
items.documentation:
The toroidal projection $\delta B_\phi = \delta\mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ of the linearized magnetic-field perturbation in the current-free vacuum surrounding the plasma constitutes one scalar component of the full perturbed vacuum magnetic-field vector. In the vacuum exterior, $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$, so $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is derivable from a scalar magnetic potential satisfying Laplace's equation; the toroidal component is determined by matching conditions at the plasma-vacuum interface and at any conducting wall boundaries. The eigenfunction is complex-valued, and this parent quantity abstracts over its two real-valued projections: [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), which carry the in-phase and quadrature contributions of the mode structure relative to the toroidal reference angle $\phi$. This projection is one component of the full [perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) vector, alongside the poloidal and radial components captured by [poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part). Computed by solving the vacuum Maxwell equations exterior to the plasma boundary in linear MHD stability analysis; the absolute amplitude is normalization-dependent, while the relative phase between vacuum and plasma regions carries reconnection information relevant to resistive and resistive-wall modes.

Sign convention: Positive when $\delta B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: radial_total_momentum_source
items.description: Signed rate of momentum input or removal per unit area in the major-radius direction, summed over all included particle populations.
items.documentation:
The radial total momentum source is the major-radius component of the net momentum-transfer rate per unit area supplied to or removed from all included particle populations. It is a directional projection of the [total momentum source](name:total_momentum_source), not a coordinate locating the momentum.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, this projection is defined by:

$$
S_R = \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{tot}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $S_R$ is the radial total momentum source, $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total momentum-source vector, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.

The total is the algebraic sum of contributions from all included particle populations, not a sum of their magnitudes. The source is area-normalized rather than a volumetric force density. The major-radius direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface; the [toroidal momentum source](name:toroidal_momentum_source) instead resolves momentum transfer along the toroidal direction.

This quantity describes gain or loss of [momentum](name:momentum) through source processes. It is distinct from [total momentum flux](name:total_momentum_flux), which describes momentum transported across an oriented surface.

Sign convention: Positive when the net source adds momentum in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.
